# Critical three-fiber cap circuits: zero drift and the covered side

Let d>=2 and let A,K,B be positive d-dimensional convex fibers at
-1,0,1 with (A+B)/2 subset K. Let y in K, and suppose finitely many
closed ambient halfspaces

    H_i={ (z,x):u_i.(x-y)+beta_i z>=0 },  u_i!=0,

all attain the same raw depth Q at (0,y), and all have exact
captured-side root equality

    |K intersect (H_i)_0|^(1/d)
       = (|A intersect (H_i)_-1|^(1/d)
                      +|B intersect (H_i)_1|^(1/d))/2.

Assume their middle traces cover K. No initial properness assumption
is necessary. The finite-tilt equalization lemma proved in
`candidate fee4b98d94ecbcf2`
forces each of the three captures of every cap to have the same
volume q=Q/3. The finite cover forces q>0. Finite saturated tilts
then give |A|,|B|>=2q, so both endpoint captures and complements have
positive volume: every endpoint cut is proper automatically.

## 1. A cap cover of all three fibers gives the full ordinary constant

If the whole family covers S, then it covers each individual fiber.
For the ordinary centroid of any one fiber, choose a member of the
family whose corresponding trace contains that centroid. Ordinary
Grunbaum gives

    q>=Gamma_d |A|, q>=Gamma_d |K|, q>=Gamma_d |B|.

Consequently M=|A|+|K|+|B|<=3q/Gamma_d and

    depth_S(0,y)=Q/M>=Gamma_d.                       (1)

This conclusion needs only the stated set cover; it does not require
any classification or global homothety of the bodies. Positive balance
of the full ambient normals is one sufficient condition for the cover,
since all cap boundaries pass through the same source point.

## 2. A continuous positive circuit identifies the potentially large side

Suppose there are positive weights lambda_i with

    sum_i lambda_i u_i=0,

and define the scalar integer-coordinate drift

    Delta=sum_i lambda_i beta_i.

No minimality or full-rank hypothesis is needed. For any point x in
the fiber at base z, its weighted sum of cap margins is exactly

    sum_i lambda_i [u_i.(x-y)+beta_i z]=z Delta.     (2)

If z Delta>=0, it is impossible for all margins to be strictly
negative. Hence that entire fiber is covered by the cap family.
The middle fiber is always covered. If Delta>0, the fiber B is
covered; if Delta<0, the fiber A is covered. If Delta=0, every fiber
is covered, and (1) applies.

Thus for Delta>0,

    |K|,|B|<=q/Gamma_d,

and only A can exceed this ordinary centroid bound. For Delta<0 the
roles reverse. This is a sign conclusion for the actual ambient
sections; no replacement by common continuous halfplanes is made.

There is an exact centroid expression for any excess. Let g_z be
the ordinary centroid of fiber C_z. If |C_z|>q/Gamma_d, then no
selected cap can contain g_z, by ordinary Grunbaum. Every margin

    m_i(z)=u_i.(g_z-y)+beta_i z

is therefore strictly negative. Summing gives

    sum_i lambda_i[-m_i(z)]=-z Delta>0.             (3)

So only the negative-drift side can have excess volume, and the
drift is exactly its weighted sum of positive centroid-to-cut
functional gaps. Dividing each term by |u_i| gives the corresponding
Euclidean signed distance, with weights lambda_i |u_i|.

## 3. Why this second covered fiber does not improve the scalar root bound

Write k=q^(1/d), c=|K|^(1/d), L=2^(1/d), and g=Gamma_d^(1/d).
The common-capture finite-tilt bounds and whole-body BM give

    |A|^(1/d),|B|^(1/d)>=Lk,
    |A|^(1/d)+|B|^(1/d)<=2c,
    c<=k/g.

The quantitative finite-tilt theorem therefore gives

    M/q<=g^(-d)+2+(2/g-L)^d.

Knowing one endpoint is covered adds an upper bound k/g on that
endpoint's root. It does not improve this scalar maximization:
the maximizing root triple allowed by these numerical constraints is

    c=k/g, covered endpoint root=Lk,
    uncovered endpoint root=2k/g-Lk.

The added covered-side constraint is satisfied because L<=1/g,
equivalently 2Gamma_d<=1. This is only an optimization of necessary
numerical constraints; it does not claim realization of that triple
by actual bodies with the critical cap structure. A stronger geometric
bound would need information beyond these scalar root and cover bounds.

All conclusions concern exactly three positive d-dimensional fibers.
They do not impose a common affine shear on a general cap family or
assert that zero drift forces global translation of the bodies.
